text: Mussolini founds the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in Milan: a small group of war veterans, nationalists, Futurists and former revolutionary syndicalists. Its first program (June 1919) mixed nationalism with radical demands such as votes for women, an eight-hour working day and a heavy tax on capital; the movement dropped most of these as it moved right in 1920–21. The word fascio means a bundle or group, recalling the Roman fasces, a bundle of rods carried before magistrates as a sign of authority.
method: Balance review: what the movement promised and who joined it, so the left/right debate has its evidence
problem: The original record gives no sense of what early Fascism promised. The 1919 program's radical demands are central evidence for the 'left or right?' debate (3B) and are used by both sides: one side sees socialist roots, the other a program abandoned once landowners and industrialists began funding the squads. Explaining the word also covers the label. New facts (June 1919 program and its demands, the 1920–21 shift) need a source, e.g. Britannica 'Fascism' or Payne 1995.

text: In Munich the German Workers’ Party, soon renamed the National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP), announces its 25-point program. It demands a Greater Germany, the overturning of the Versailles treaty, and citizenship only for people of ‘German blood’, stating outright that no Jew can belong to the nation. Its economic points include nationalizing trusts, profit-sharing in large firms and land reform; in 1928 Hitler stated that the land point was aimed only at Jewish speculators. Historians still argue over how seriously the economic points were meant (debate 3B).
method: Balance review: settled antisemitic core stated plainly; both sides of the left/right debate get their evidence
problem: The original omits the program's explicit exclusion of Jews (point 4), which is a settled fact and should be stated plainly. It also lists only one economic demand, so neither side of debate 3B gets its evidence: the 'socialist' reading relies on these points, and the 'right' reading relies on Hitler's 1928 reinterpretation and on the points being dropped in power. New facts (point 4 wording in paraphrase, profit-sharing, land reform, the 1928 clarification of point 17) are all in the GHDI program text and standard histories (Evans 2003). Add GHDI as a source.

text: Fascist squads converge on Rome. King Victor Emmanuel III declines to sign a martial-law decree that the army was ready to enforce, and appoints Mussolini prime minister of a coalition government. Historians debate why: fear of civil war, doubts about the army's loyalty, and pressure from nationalists, business leaders and conservatives who saw Mussolini as a barrier to socialism are all cited. In form the appointment was legal; in practice it followed a threat of force and two years of squad violence against socialists, unions and local councils.
method: Balance review: explains why the King gave way and how the appointment was both legal in form and coerced in practice
problem: The original reads as a neutral handover and does not explain why. The causes (elite choice, fear of the left, squad violence across 1920–22) are central to Paxton's 'stage three' and to the 'coup or not?' true/false card, which should not be answered with a flat 'false' (see .md, section 4). New facts need a source, e.g. Bosworth, Mussolini's Italy (2005) or Paxton (2004).

text: Hitler and the Nazis try to seize power in Munich. Bavarian police stop the march with gunfire; four policemen and fourteen putschists die, and the putsch fails. Hitler is tried for treason. The court gives him the minimum sentence of five years and he is released after about nine months, during which he writes the first volume of Mein Kampf. The Nazis later honoured their dead from the putsch as martyrs.
method: Balance review: explains leniency of the courts (an institutional cause) and later propaganda use
problem: Adds the 'why': a lenient, sympathetic court is a standard example of how Weimar justice treated the nationalist right far more mildly than the left. It also explains the later 'martyr' cult instead of leaving it unexplained. Death toll and sentence details need a source (Britannica, Beer Hall Putsch; Kershaw, Hitler vol. 1). The original's 'Police stop the march' is kept.

text: A squad of Fascist militants led by Amerigo Dumini kidnaps and murders the Socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti after he denounces Fascist violence and fraud in the 1924 election. In the crisis that follows, opposition deputies walk out of parliament (the ‘Aventine secession’), but the King does not act. In January 1925 Mussolini tells parliament he takes responsibility for what happened and then builds an open dictatorship over the next two years.
method: Balance review: removes loaded wording ('thugs') and explains why the crisis ended in dictatorship
problem: 'Fascist thugs' is a loaded label (STANDARDS §1); name the group and its leader instead. Adds the opposition's response and the King's inaction, which explain why the crisis ended in dictatorship. Dumini and the Aventine secession need a source (Britannica, Giacomo Matteotti).

text: To crush armed resistance in Cyrenaica led by Omar al-Mukhtar, Italian forces deport 100,000–110,000 people, mostly women, children and the elderly, into desert concentration camps. The regime called the campaign ‘pacification’. Estimates of deaths in the deportations and camps range from about 40,000 to 70,000. Al-Mukhtar was captured and publicly hanged in 1931. Whether the campaign was genocide is debated: Ali Abdullatif Ahmida (2020) argues it was; other historians call it an extreme colonial counter-insurgency, comparable to other empires' campaigns of the period.
method: Balance review: victims and resisters named; official euphemism given context; genocide label shown as debated, not decided
problem: The original names no Libyan actor and no debate, though the brief marks 'genocide' as contested. The regime's own word 'pacification' needs context. The comparison with other empires' counter-insurgency is part of the same-standard rule (§1) and should cross-link to the capitalism/empire pages. Al-Mukhtar and the debate need sources (Ahmida 2020; a counter-view, e.g. Rochat or Bosworth).

text: President Paul von Hindenburg appoints Hitler chancellor at the head of a coalition with the conservative German National People’s Party, with Franz von Papen as vice chancellor. Nazis hold only three of the eleven cabinet posts, and Papen and his conservative allies believed they could control Hitler. Within months the Nazis had pushed them aside.
method: Balance review: explains elite miscalculation, a central cause in every school
problem: The record needs the 'why': conservative elites chose Hitler believing they could contain him (Paxton's stage three; debate 3E 'elite decisions'). Three of eleven posts (Hitler, Frick, Göring) is standard (Evans 2003; USHMM).

text: The Reichstag building burns. A young Dutch former Communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, is arrested at the scene and later executed. The Nazis claim it is the signal for a Communist uprising, and the next day an emergency decree suspends basic civil rights; the regime uses it to arrest thousands of Communists and other opponents. Whether van der Lubbe acted alone (Fritz Tobias, Hans Mommsen) or Nazis were involved (Benjamin Carter Hett, 2014) is still debated by historians.
method: Balance review: contested question presented with both schools; propaganda claim given context
problem: Who set the fire is a genuinely open historical question and should be presented with both schools named; the original is silent on it, which leaves readers to fill the gap with myths from either side. The Nazi claim of a Communist uprising is the propaganda use that needs context. Sources: USHMM 'Reichstag Fire'; Hett, Burning the Reichstag (2014); Tobias (1962).

text: In the last multi-party Reichstag election of the Nazi era, held amid arrests and intimidation of opponents, the Nazis win almost 44 percent (43.9 in the official count). With their conservative partners the coalition passes 50 percent.
method: Balance review: wording
problem: 'Before the war' is misleading (there was no other multi-party election until 1949); wording change only.

text: The Reichstag passes the Enabling Act by 444 votes to 94, letting the government make laws without parliament. The Communist deputies had been arrested or driven into hiding, armed SA and SS men filled the building, and the rules were changed so that absent deputies counted as present. The Catholic Centre Party and the other non-socialist parties voted yes after promises from Hitler; only the Social Democrats voted no.
method: Balance review: collaboration by democratic parties stated plainly; causal overclaim removed
problem: The original ('passes only because opposition deputies were arrested...') leaves out that the Centre Party and liberal parties voted for it. That omission lets democratic parties off the hook and hides one of the main lessons historians draw (democratic parties voting away democracy). It also makes an unsourced causal claim. Vote count and Centre vote: USHMM 'Enabling Act'; Evans 2003.

text: Italy invades Ethiopia, a fellow member of the League of Nations, and takes Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936; League sanctions fail. Italian forces use chemical weapons, chiefly mustard gas dropped and sprayed from aircraft, in breach of the 1925 Geneva Protocol. Emperor Haile Selassie appeals to the League in person in June 1936; Ethiopian fighters (the Arbegnoch, or patriots) keep up resistance until British and Ethiopian forces drive Italy out in 1941. The war was popular in Italy, where the regime presented it as winning a place in the sun and avenging the defeat at Adwa (1896). Italy officially admitted using gas only in the mid-1990s.
method: Balance review: victims and resistance named; why it was popular in Italy explained
problem: The original has no Ethiopian actors, no resistance and no 'why' for Italian support. Adds the regime's justifications (with who said them) and the late admission. New facts need sources: Britannica Italo-Ethiopian War (League appeal, 1941); Del Boca for the 1995–96 admission (already a to-fetch item in the brief).

text: Army officers including Francisco Franco rise against Spain’s elected Popular Front government, starting the Spanish Civil War. The rebels said they were acting to stop disorder, attacks on the Catholic Church and a feared revolution, pointing to the murder of the monarchist leader José Calvo Sotelo by Republican police and militants on 13 July. Defenders of the Republic answer that it was a lawful, elected government and that the coup itself set off the revolution and the war. Germany and Italy send troops, aircraft and tanks to the Nationalists; the Soviet Union supplies the Republic, and Britain and France adopt non-intervention.
method: Balance review: both sides' stated reasons for the war given at their strongest
problem: Why the war began is one of the most contested questions in Spanish history (Payne and Álvarez Tardío vs Preston, Casanova and Viñas). The original gives only the Republic's framing. Each side's case is now given in its own terms without the site ruling. Calvo Sotelo killing and non-intervention: Britannica 'Spanish Civil War'; Payne, The Collapse of the Spanish Republic (2006); Preston, The Spanish Civil War (2006).

text: After a grenade attack on Viceroy Rodolfo Graziani by two young Eritreans, Italian soldiers, Fascist Blackshirt militia and Italian civilians kill residents across Addis Ababa for three days. Estimates of the dead range from about 3,000 (the Italian historian Angelo Del Boca and the British writer Anthony Mockler) to about 19,000 (Ian Campbell, 2017) and 30,000 (Ethiopian sources). In May 1937 Italian forces also shot the monks of the Debre Libanos monastery.
method: Balance review: fact error on Mockler; ordinary participants and named victims added
problem: Fact error: Anthony Mockler is a British writer, not an Italian historian. Balance: the participation of Italian civilians (in Campbell and Bosworth) belongs in the record, as it shows ordinary people taking part, and Debre Libanos is a named victim group. 'Blackshirt' is explained by context. Sources: History Today review (Bosworth) of Campbell; Campbell 2017.

text: Aircraft of the German Condor Legion, with Italian planes, bomb the Basque town of Guernica (Gernika) on a market day, killing many civilians. The toll is disputed: the Basque government reported 1,654 deaths; later local research has documented about 120 to 250 or more; Xabier Irujo argues for a much higher figure. Franco's side claimed that retreating Republican forces had burned the town, and the regime did not admit the bombing for decades. Picasso's painting made Guernica a worldwide symbol.
method: Balance review: internal inconsistency fixed; regime denial and propaganda use stated
problem: 'Killing hundreds' conflicts with the lower documented estimates the record itself gives; use neutral wording. The denial by Franco's regime is a key propaganda fact the brief mentions but the record omits. Picasso's Guernica is in copyright: link to the Museo Reina Sofía, do not copy the image. Sources: ENRS; The Volunteer (Irujo).

text: After capturing Nanjing, Japanese troops kill prisoners of war and civilians on a mass scale, with widespread sexual violence against women and girls, and looting. Most estimates of the Chinese dead range from 100,000 to more than 300,000; the range depends partly on the area, period and categories counted. A group of foreign residents, led by the German businessman John Rabe, ran a Safety Zone that sheltered about 200,000 or more civilians. Denial of the massacre by some Japanese writers is not a scholarly side; historians who give lower estimates, such as Hata Ikuhiko, still document mass killing.
method: Balance review: rescuers added; low estimates separated from denial; age-appropriate wording
problem: Adds rescuers (parity with the European rescuer records), and separates low estimators from deniers so neither is confused with the other. 'Sexual violence against women and girls' is suitable for the 10+ beginner layer while staying factual. Safety Zone figure: Rabe's own estimate; source Britannica or Yale Divinity Library Nanking Massacre Project.

text: German troops enter Austria unopposed and large crowds welcome Hitler in Vienna; Germany annexes the country (the Anschluss). Violence against Austrian Jews, including forced public humiliation, beatings and looting, follows at once. A plebiscite in April 1938, held under heavy pressure and with Jews and opponents excluded, reports 99.7 percent approval. After 1945 Austria long described itself as Hitler's ‘first victim’; in 1991 Chancellor Franz Vranitzky acknowledged that Austrians also shared responsibility for Nazi crimes.
method: Balance review: popular support and later memory politics added; 'first victim' label given context
problem: The original omits both the popular welcome (a key 'why' fact) and Austria's postwar 'first victim' narrative, a label that needs context and is part of the memory-politics sub-tab every case should have. Sources: USHMM 'Austria'; Vranitzky statement of 8 July 1991.

text: Britain, France, Germany and Italy agree at Munich that Czechoslovakia must cede the Sudetenland to Germany; Czechoslovakia is not party to the decision, nor is the Soviet Union. British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain says it means ‘peace for our time’. Poland and Hungary also take Czechoslovak territory in the following weeks. Whether appeasement was a grave mistake or a rational way to buy time to rearm is still debated (debate F).
method: Balance review: links to debate F without picking a side; same-standard rule for other states
problem: Link to the appeasement debate without the site deciding it; adds Poland's and Hungary's gains (same standard for every country). Sources: Britannica 'Munich Agreement'; Evans's summary of the historiography.

text: Fascist Italy passes racial laws that expel Jews from schools, universities, the civil service and the armed forces and ban marriages between Jews and other Italians. Many Italian Jews had been Fascist party members, and the laws shocked them. Historians once tended to see the laws as Mussolini copying Hitler to please his ally (Renzo De Felice); later research, notably Michele Sarfatti's, stresses the Fascist regime's own racist and antisemitic motives, already visible in its colonial laws.
method: Balance review: debate over origins shown with both schools
problem: The origin of the 1938 laws is a real debate (De Felice vs Sarfatti and others) that bears on the 'Italian Fascism was mild' myth. Both views now shown. Sources: Sarfatti, The Jews in Mussolini's Italy (2006); De Felice, Storia degli ebrei italiani sotto il fascismo (1961).

text: Using the shooting of the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris by Herschel Grynszpan, a young Polish Jew whose family had just been expelled from Germany, as a pretext, the regime organizes a pogrom across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland. Propaganda presented it as spontaneous popular anger; in fact party and SA leaders, urged on by Goebbels, organized it. More than 1,400 synagogues are burned or destroyed, thousands of Jewish businesses are wrecked, at least 91 Jews are killed and hundreds more die after arrest or by suicide, and about 26,000–30,000 Jewish men are sent to concentration camps. The state then fines German Jews one billion Reichsmarks. Many historians now prefer the name ‘November pogrom’, because ‘Kristallnacht’ (night of broken glass) makes it sound as if only property was damaged.
method: Balance review: label and propaganda framing given context; documented death toll
problem: The label 'Kristallnacht' needs context (§1). The regime's 'spontaneous' framing is propaganda that must be shown with what the evidence shows. 'Hundreds of Jews die' should give the documented figure (USHMM: at least 91 killed during the pogrom). Grynszpan's motive (the Polenaktion expulsions) is part of the 'why'. Sources: USHMM 'Kristallnacht'.

text: Madrid falls and Franco declares the civil war over; about 500,000 people died in the war. Killings behind the lines took place on both sides. In the Republican zone about 50,000 people were killed, mostly in the first months of the war, by militias and revolutionary committees; the victims included about 6,800 priests, monks and nuns, and thousands of prisoners taken from Madrid jails and shot at Paracuellos in late 1936. The Republican government gradually brought these killings under control. On the Nationalist side, killing was a policy ordered by the rebel commanders; historians estimate Nationalist and Francoist killings during and after the war at about 130,000–150,000 or more, with executions continuing for years after 1939 and hundreds of thousands held in prisons and camps. About 450,000 Spaniards fled to France in early 1939.
method: Balance review: Republican-zone killings stated factually with named victims; asymmetry stated without false equivalence
problem: The original gives the Republican-zone figure as a bare number and no victims; the brief's own task list asks for communist and anti-fascist violence to be stated factually. This names the victims (clergy, Paracuellos) without false equivalence: the asymmetry in scale, organization and duration is stated plainly, as most historians across schools (Preston, Casanova, Payne, Ledesma) accept. Clergy figure: Antonio Montero Moreno (1961), 6,832. Paracuellos and exile figures need sources (Preston 2012; Payne 2012; Ledesma). Note: Preston's title 'The Spanish Holocaust' is itself criticized (e.g. by Payne) for borrowing the word; cite the title, but do not use the phrase in the site's own voice.

text: Germany invades Poland, starting the Second World War in Europe; Britain and France declare war on 3 September. Under a secret protocol of the Nazi–Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939, the Soviet Union invades eastern Poland on 17 September, and the two powers divide the country.
method: Balance review: same standard: Soviet role added
problem: Same standard for every side (§1): the Soviet invasion under the secret protocol belongs in the same record. Sources: Britannica 'German-Soviet Nonaggression Pact'; Avalon Project text of the secret protocol.

text: Hitler secretly authorizes the murder of institutionalized disabled people, backdating the order to 1 September 1939. The regime called it ‘euthanasia’ (mercy killing), but the victims were not dying and did not consent; they were killed because the regime judged their lives ‘unworthy of life’. T4’s own count is 70,273 people gassed in six centers by August 1941. After public protests, including a sermon by Bishop Clemens August von Galen of Münster in August 1941, the gassing in those centers was stopped, but killing by starvation, drugs and shooting went on; historians estimate about 250,000 victims across all phases.
method: Balance review: perpetrator euphemism given context; resistance and its limits added
problem: 'Euthanasia' is the perpetrators' euphemism and must not stand without context (§1). Galen's protest is a key example of resistance that had an effect, and of what was learned about public pressure. Sources: USHMM 'Euthanasia Program'; USHMM on Galen.

text: The first Polish prisoners arrive at Auschwitz, a camp the SS set up that spring. Auschwitz grew into the largest killing site of the Holocaust, where about 1.1 million people were killed: about 1 million Jews, and also about 70,000–75,000 non-Jewish Poles, about 21,000 Roma and Sinti, about 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war and some 10,000–15,000 others.
method: Balance review: names all victim groups
problem: Names the non-Jewish victim groups of Auschwitz, which the original's 'about 1 million of them Jews' leaves anonymous. Figures are the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum / Franciszek Piper estimates; add that source.

text: After France’s defeat, parliament votes 569 to 80 to give Marshal Philippe Pétain, the most admired French commander of the First World War, full powers, and the Vichy regime replaces the Republic. Pétain promised a ‘National Revolution’ under the motto ‘Work, Family, Fatherland’, and many French people, shocked by defeat, at first trusted him. In October 1940 Vichy issues, on its own initiative, a Statute on Jews excluding them from public service and many professions, extended in June 1941.
method: Balance review: why people supported Vichy; slogan with context
problem: Adds why many French people supported Vichy (defeat trauma, Pétain's prestige) and gives its slogans with context, as §1 requires for labels. The 569–80 vote shows the Republic's own parliament ended it. Sources: Paxton, Vichy France (1972); Britannica 'Vichy France'.

text: Romania’s Iron Guard rises against its partner in government, General Ion Antonescu. Antonescu crushes the revolt with German army support. During the revolt Guardists carry out a pogrom in Bucharest in which about 120–125 Jews are murdered.
method: Balance review: toll understated
problem: 'Dozens' understates the documented toll (usually given as about 125, e.g. the Wiesel Commission and standard summaries). Fact-checker to confirm the exact figure against the Wiesel Commission report.

text: After the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia, Germany and Italy set up the Independent State of Croatia with Ante Pavelić and the Ustaše in power. Some Croats at first welcomed independence after two decades in a Serb-dominated kingdom; the Ustaše regime then persecuted and murdered Serbs, Jews and Roma, and also killed Croat and Muslim opponents, while also forcing many Serbs to convert to Catholicism.
method: Balance review: causes, sponsors and all victim groups
problem: Adds the 'why' (interwar grievances), the Axis sponsors, and the regime's Croat and Muslim victims and forced conversions. The wider Yugoslav war also included mass killings of Muslims and Croats by Serbian Chetniks and postwar killings by Tito's Partisans (Bleiburg); these need their own records (see .md gaps). Sources: Tomasevich (2001); USHMM 'Croatia'.

text: Germany and its allies invade the Soviet Union in a war the regime planned as a war of annihilation. SS and police units (Einsatzgruppen), with army support and local auxiliaries, begin mass shootings of Jews behind the front, and army orders such as the Commissar Order told troops to shoot Soviet political officers on capture.
method: Balance review: army's role, against the 'clean Wehrmacht' myth
problem: Adds the army's role. The postwar claim of a 'clean Wehrmacht' that took no part in crimes was widely believed in West Germany and was overturned by research and the 1995 Wehrmacht exhibition; the record should not leave room for it. Source: USHMM 'Operation Barbarossa' or Bundesarchiv; Hamburg Institute exhibition catalogue.

text: The Ustaše run the Jasenovac camp complex, where USHMM estimates 77,000–99,000 people were murdered: 45,000–52,000 Serbs, 12,000–20,000 Jews, 15,000–20,000 Roma and 5,000–12,000 Croat and Muslim opponents. The Jasenovac Memorial Site's list of named victims supports this order of magnitude. Postwar Yugoslav and later Serbian nationalist figures of 500,000–700,000 or more, and Croatian nationalist claims that minimize or deny the killing, are both rejected by researchers using name lists.
method: Balance review: names each competing claim and the method used to test it
problem: The original 'much higher and much lower figures circulate for political reasons' asserts a motive without saying who or what. Naming each claim and the method that tests it is fairer and more instructive. Minimization that denies the killing is denial and is not presented as a side. Source for the name list to fetch (brief task 5).

text: At the Babi Yar (Babyn Yar) ravine outside Kyiv, SS and police units, guided by Einsatzgruppe C and helped by Ukrainian auxiliary police, shoot 33,771 Jews in two days, according to their own reports. In the months that followed Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, psychiatric patients and others were also killed there; Soviet investigators later estimated about 100,000 people were killed at the site. Soviet memorials long avoided saying that most victims were Jews.
method: Balance review: collaborators and all victim groups; memory politics
problem: Adds the local auxiliaries (equal rigor on collaborators across nations), the other victim groups, and Soviet memory politics. Sources: USHMM 'Kiev and Babi Yar'; Babyn Yar Holocaust Memorial Center.

text: In Operation Reinhard, named after Reinhard Heydrich, the SS murders Jews of occupied Poland in three killing centers: about 925,000 at Treblinka, 434,508 at Belzec and at least 167,000 at Sobibor (USHMM estimates). Prisoners revolted at Treblinka in August 1943 and at Sobibor in October 1943; some hundreds escaped, and a few dozen survived the war from each camp.
method: Balance review: victims' resistance added
problem: Adds the prisoner revolts (resistance by victims, §2). Survivor numbers need sourcing (USHMM 'Sobibor', 'Treblinka').

text: French police arrest about 13,000 Jews in Paris, about 4,000 of them children, and hold many in the Vélodrome d’Hiver before deportation to Auschwitz; very few survived. The police had planned to arrest about 27,000; many others escaped after warnings, some of them from police officers and neighbours. In 1995 President Jacques Chirac acknowledged the French state’s responsibility.
method: Balance review: bystanders and rescuers; memory politics
problem: Adds the warnings and escape (ordinary people's choices) and France's later acknowledgment (memory). Sources: USHMM 'Vél d'Hiv'; Chirac speech of 16 July 1995.

text: Hans Scholl, Sophie Scholl and Christoph Probst of the White Rose, a student resistance group in Munich that distributed anti-Nazi leaflets, are executed days after their arrest. Other German resistance came from Communists, Social Democrats and trade unionists, who filled the first camps in 1933, from church members, and from individuals such as Georg Elser, who tried to kill Hitler with a bomb in November 1939.
method: Balance review: parity across resisters of different politics
problem: The record set has no record of left-wing or working-class German resistance, which was the largest early resistance and the first target of terror; the only German resistance records are students and officers. Either broaden this record or add separate records (see .md). Sources: German Resistance Memorial Center (Gedenkstätte Deutscher Widerstand).

text: Jewish fighters of the Jewish Combat Organization (ŻOB), led by Mordechai Anielewicz, and the Jewish Military Union (ŻZW) resist the final deportations from the Warsaw ghetto for nearly a month, the largest Jewish uprising of the war. German forces burn the ghetto block by block; the SS commander Jürgen Stroop reported more than 56,000 Jews captured, and most survivors were deported to Treblinka and other camps.
method: Balance review: resisters named
problem: Names the fighters and both organizations (victims and resisters named where known, §4). Stroop's report figure needs a source (USHMM 'Warsaw Ghetto Uprising'). The Stroop Report photos are perpetrator-made: show only with context (see .md).

text: Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg sets off a bomb at Hitler’s headquarters in East Prussia; Hitler survives, the coup fails, and the regime executes many of the conspirators and arrests thousands of suspects. The plotters were mostly conservative and nationalist officers and officials; some had served the regime for years. Historians debate the mix of motives: moral revulsion at its crimes, the wish to save Germany from total defeat, or both.
method: Balance review: motives debate added
problem: The record says nothing about who the plotters were or why. Their motives are debated (e.g. Hans Mommsen, Peter Hoffmann, Christian Gerlach on some plotters' roles in the East). Presenting the debate avoids both hero-worship and dismissal. Sources: German Resistance Memorial Center; Hoffmann, The History of the German Resistance.

text: With German backing, the Arrow Cross under Ferenc Szálasi takes power in Hungary. Arrow Cross militias murder thousands of Jews in Budapest, many shot on the banks of the Danube, and force tens of thousands on marches toward the Austrian border. Diplomats including Raoul Wallenberg, Carl Lutz of Switzerland and Giorgio Perlasca issued protective papers to save as many as they could.
method: Balance review: rescuers added
problem: Adds rescuers alongside perpetrators. Victim figures (often given as 10,000–15,000 or more killed in Budapest by Arrow Cross men) need a source (USHMM 'Hungary after the German Occupation'). The Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial is a good archive seed.

text: Italian partisans capture Mussolini near Dongo as he tries to flee to Switzerland in German uniform, and shoot him and his companion Clara Petacci at Giulino di Mezzegra by Lake Como. Their bodies are hung up in Milan’s Piazzale Loreto, where Fascist forces had displayed the bodies of 15 executed partisans in August 1944. In the weeks after the war partisans and others also killed thousands of Fascists and suspected collaborators; the number is debated.
method: Balance review: anti-fascist violence stated factually; no photos
problem: Covers anti-fascist violence factually (task requirement): the killing of Petacci, the public display, and the 1945 revenge killings, whose toll is debated (figures and authors to fetch, e.g. Mirco Dondi; Giampaolo Pansa's popular books on the other side). The Piazzale Loreto precedent explains the choice of place without justifying it. No images of the bodies.

text: The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg tries 22 leading Nazis on four counts, including crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Nineteen are convicted, 12 of them sentenced to death, and three are acquitted. Critics then and since have called it victors’ justice: Allied conduct was not judged, and the Soviet prosecutors even charged Germany with the Katyn massacre of Polish officers, which Soviet forces had carried out. Defenders point to the mass of documentary evidence, the defense lawyers and the acquittals, and to the trial's lasting role in international law.
method: Balance review: critics and defenders both shown
problem: Critics of the trial are not given at all; the 'victors' justice' critique (including from some Allied lawyers and judges) is a serious position and should be shown with its defenders' answer. The Katyn charge is a documented fact (dropped from the judgment). Sources: Avalon Project IMT records; Britannica 'Nürnberg trials'; for Katyn, USHMM or the IMT record.

text: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East tries Japanese wartime leaders; seven, including Tōjō Hideki, are hanged on 23 December 1948. The United States decided not to indict Emperor Hirohito; how much responsibility he bore is debated (Herbert Bix argues a great deal; others stress the military's control). The Indian judge Radhabinod Pal dissented, voting to acquit all defendants: he accepted that atrocities such as those at Nanjing happened, but argued that the charge of aggressive war was retroactive law and that the Western powers were judging others for what they had done in their own empires. His dissent is still cited by Japanese nationalists and criticized by many historians.
method: Balance review: dissent explained in its own terms; emperor debate shown
problem: Pal's dissent is mentioned without its reasoning, which invites misreading in both directions (it is widely quoted as if Pal denied the atrocities). Hirohito's responsibility is a real debate. Sources: Pal's dissenting judgment; Bix, Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan (2000); a counter-view (e.g. Peter Wetzler or Noriko Kawamura).

text: Ion Antonescu, Romania’s wartime dictator, is executed after a trial by a Romanian people’s tribunal for war crimes, including the murder of Jews. The tribunal sat under Soviet occupation and growing Communist control, which later critics used to question its fairness. In the 1990s some Romanian nationalists tried to rehabilitate Antonescu; in 2004 the international Wiesel Commission, set up by the Romanian state, confirmed his regime's responsibility for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Jews and Roma.
method: Balance review: critics' view of the trial and memory politics, crimes kept plain
problem: Adds context on the tribunal (critics' point stated) and on postwar memory, without casting doubt on the crimes. Sources: Wiesel Commission Final Report (2004); USHMM 'Romania'.

text: Former members of Mussolini’s movement, among them officials of the Salò Republic such as Giorgio Almirante, found the Italian Social Movement (MSI), postwar Italy’s main neo-fascist party. In 1995 its successor, National Alliance, formally renounced fascism. Brothers of Italy, founded in 2012 by former National Alliance members, describes itself as a conservative party; critics point to its roots in the MSI and to the tricolour flame it kept in its logo.
method: Balance review: modern party shown through its own statements and critics' only
problem: 'Today's Brothers of Italy descends from it' is lineage, but presented alone it reads as a label. STANDARDS rule for modern parties: their own statements plus their critics'. Sources: Britannica 'Italian Social Movement'; FdI statute/party site for its self-description; a critic (e.g. a journalist or historian) for the flame symbol.

text: A Soviet court at Khabarovsk tries 12 former members of Japan’s Kwantung Army and Unit 731 for biological warfare. Western governments dismissed the trial at the time as Soviet propaganda; later research confirmed much of its evidence. Unit members who had returned to Japan were never prosecuted; US investigators had obtained their data in exchange for immunity.
method: Balance review: reception and later evidence added
problem: Adds how the trial was received and how its evidence fared, a source-criticism lesson (Clouded at the time, Strong now). Source: Tsuneishi (2005) already cited; Harris, Factories of Death.

text: Adolf Eichmann, captured in Argentina by Israeli agents in May 1960, is tried in Jerusalem, where survivor testimony is central. Argentina protested that the capture broke its sovereignty, and the UN Security Council asked Israel to make reparation. He is convicted and sentenced to death, and is hanged on 1 June 1962.
method: Balance review: legal controversy stated
problem: Adds Argentina's protest and UN Security Council resolution 138 (1960), so the legal controversy is shown factually. Source: UN Security Council resolution 138.

text: Francisco Franco dies in office after 36 years of rule. Spain moves to democracy under King Juan Carlos. A 1977 amnesty law, demanded at the time by the left to free political prisoners and passed by a large majority, also shields crimes of the dictatorship from prosecution; United Nations human rights bodies have since said it should not cover crimes against humanity, while its defenders say it was the foundation of a peaceful transition.
method: Balance review: both sides of the amnesty debate
problem: The 1977 law is presented only as shielding crimes. Its history (freeing anti-Franco prisoners, broad support including the Communist Party) and the present debate need both sides. Sources: text of Ley 46/1977; UN Human Rights Committee or Special Rapporteur reports on Spain.

text: The historians’ dispute (Historikerstreit) breaks out in West Germany after Ernst Nolte suggests that Nazi crimes were in part a reaction to Bolshevik terror, which he called their precedent. Nolte and some defenders said Nazism must be historicized and compared like any other past. Jürgen Habermas and most historians rejected his causal claim as relativizing the Holocaust; comparison of Nazi and Soviet crimes nonetheless became normal scholarship.
method: Balance review: both positions in their own terms
problem: Gives Nolte's position in his own terms and the outcome, as the brief does, instead of only the rejection.

text: Spain’s government exhumes Franco’s remains from the state mausoleum at the Valley of the Fallen, built in part with the labour of Republican political prisoners and renamed the Valley of Cuelgamuros in 2022, and reburies them in a family plot after a long legal fight with his descendants. Supporters said a democracy should not honour a dictator in a state monument; opponents, including his family and some conservatives, said it reopened old wounds.
method: Balance review: label context; both sides
problem: 'Valley of the Fallen' is the Francoist name; give its context and the current name. Both sides' reasons stated. Sources: Spanish Democratic Memory Law (renaming); Britannica or a major newspaper on the exhumation and the forced-labour history.

text: Spain’s Democratic Memory Law comes into force, making the state responsible for searching for and exhuming people who disappeared in the Civil War and under Franco. Supporters say families have a right to find and bury their dead. The People’s Party and Vox oppose it, saying it reopens old wounds, breaks the spirit of the 1977 reconciliation and treats history one-sidedly; the 1977 amnesty law still blocks prosecutions.
method: Balance review: both sides in their own terms
problem: 'Conservative parties oppose it' gives no reasons; §1 requires their reasoning in their own terms, and supporters' reasons too.

text: Giorgia Meloni of Brothers of Italy, a party whose roots go back through National Alliance to the neo-fascist MSI, is sworn in as Italy’s first woman prime minister. She describes her party as conservative, has said fascism belongs to history, and has called the 1938 racial laws the low point of Italian history. Critics point to the party’s roots and symbols and to her refusal to describe herself as anti-fascist.
method: Balance review: modern party: own statements and critics' only
problem: Already follows the rule (own statements plus critics'). Small changes: lineage stated precisely, the party's self-description added, the critics' points made specific. The critics' last point needs a source.

text: Germany’s domestic intelligence agency (BfV) classifies the AfD party as ‘confirmed right-wing extremist’, saying its ethnic idea of the German people is incompatible with human dignity, then suspends the label pending a court case. The AfD calls itself a democratic, patriotic party and calls the classification politically motivated. In February 2026 the Cologne Administrative Court bars the classification for now in a ruling that is not final. ‘Extremist’ in German constitutional law is a legal category; it is not the same as calling a party fascist.
method: Balance review: modern party: own statement, authority's reasoning, court's ruling; no site label
problem: The original gives the authority's action but not the party's own statement or the agency's reasoning, and lacks the brief's note that 'extremist' is not 'fascist'. Sources: BfV press release of 2 May 2025; AfD statement; the court ruling (already cited).

text: Former socialist editor who founded Fascism in 1919, became prime minister in 1922 and dictator by 1925, and allied Italy with Nazi Germany. He was called Il Duce (‘the leader’, from the Latin dux), the title at the centre of a personality cult built by the regime; supporters at home and some admirers abroad praised him in the 1920s for restoring order, while opponents were beaten, jailed, exiled to remote islands or killed. Deposed in 1943, he was shot by partisans in April 1945.
method: Balance review: leader title with full context
problem: 'Il Duce' is the textbook example of a label that must not appear without context (§1). Adds what the title meant to supporters and what critics and evidence show. Sources: Bosworth (2005); Britannica.

text: Leader of the Nazi Party from 1921 and dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945. After President Hindenburg died in August 1934 he merged the offices of chancellor and president and took the title Führer (‘leader’), to whom soldiers and officials swore personal oaths; the regime's propaganda presented him as the nation's saviour. He started the Second World War in Europe and drove the genocide of European Jews and other mass murders.
method: Balance review: leader title with full context
problem: 'Führer' appears in the brief and on the site; give it context once, in the person record (§1).

text: General who led the Nationalist side in the Spanish Civil War with German and Italian help and ruled Spain as dictator from 1939 until his death, with the title Caudillo (‘leader’), which his regime used to present him as the saviour of Catholic Spain. Supporters credit him with keeping Spain out of the Second World War and with the economic growth of the 1960s; critics point to mass executions, prisons and labour camps, and decades of repression. Whether his regime was fascist or authoritarian-conservative is debated.
method: Balance review: honorific with context; supporters and critics
problem: '(Caudillo)' is an unexplained honorific (§1). Supporters' and critics' cases added in their own terms. Note for the fact-checker: Spain was neutral/'non-belligerent', but sent the Blue Division to fight the Soviet Union (1941–43); add that to keep the 'kept Spain out' claim honest. Sources: Payne (1987); Preston, Franco (1993).

text: Founder of the Ustaše movement and head of the Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945, with the title Poglavnik (‘leader’). His regime murdered Serbs, Jews and Roma as well as Croat and Muslim opponents. He escaped in 1948 to Argentina through the ‘ratlines’, escape routes run with help from some Catholic clergy in Rome, and died in Madrid in 1959.
method: Balance review: title with context; escape route explained
problem: '(Poglavnik)' is an unexplained title; 'ratlines' and the clergy's role are factual context (Phayer, Pius XII, the Holocaust, and the Cold War, 2008; Tomasevich 2001).

text: Army general and prime minister of Japan from October 1941 to July 1944, who led the country into war with the United States and Britain. He was convicted by the Tokyo tribunal and hanged in 1948. In 1978 he and other convicted leaders were enshrined at the Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo, so visits there by Japanese prime ministers draw protests from China and South Korea; visitors say they honour all of Japan's war dead.
method: Balance review: memory politics with both sides
problem: Adds memory politics with both sides' statements (the Japan case needs the same 'how it is remembered' sub-tab as the others). Source: Britannica 'Yasukuni Shrine'.

text: Idealist philosopher who served as Mussolini’s education minister and wrote the philosophical section of The Doctrine of Fascism (1932), published under Mussolini’s name. He supported the German-backed Salò Republic and was killed in Florence in April 1944 by a communist partisan unit (GAP); the killing was debated even within the Resistance.
method: Balance review: anti-fascist violence stated factually
problem: Who killed him and why matters for the anti-fascist violence item: stated factually. 'Debated within the Resistance' needs a source (Italian historiography, e.g. Luciano Canfora, La sentenza, 1985).

text: Chief of the Reich Security Main Office who organized the Einsatzgruppen and chaired the Wannsee Conference; he was a main architect of what the Nazis called the ‘Final Solution of the Jewish Question’, their euphemism for the murder of Europe’s Jews. Czechoslovak parachutists attacked him in Prague and he died in June 1942; German reprisals included the destruction of the village of Lidice, where the men were shot and most of the children murdered.
method: Balance review: perpetrator euphemism given context; victims named
problem: 'Final Solution' is a perpetrator euphemism and must be explained the first time it appears (§1); the Lidice victims are named as a group. Sources: USHMM 'Lidice'; USHMM 'Final Solution'.

text: SS officer who organized the deportation of Jews from across Europe to ghettos and killing centers. Seized in Argentina in 1960, he was tried in Jerusalem and hanged in 1962. Hannah Arendt's report on the trial described him as a thoughtless functionary and coined the phrase ‘the banality of evil’; later research using his own writings and interviews in Argentina (Bettina Stangneth, David Cesarani) showed him to be a convinced antisemite.
method: Balance review: one-liner given context and evidence
problem: The 'banality of evil' phrase is a famous one-liner; it appears in the Arendt record but should be linked here too, with the evidence that challenged it.

text: Founder in 1927 of the antisemitic Legion of the Archangel Michael, later known as the Iron Guard, which mixed nationalism with Orthodox religious mysticism and political murder, including the assassination of Prime Minister Ion Duca in 1933. It drew real support from students, priests and peasants, winning about 16 percent of the vote in 1937. He was killed in custody on the orders of King Carol II’s government in 1938; officials said he was shot while trying to escape.
method: Balance review: support base and violence; attributed official version
problem: Adds the 'why' (who supported it and how much) and the movement's own violence; gives the official version of his death with attribution. Sources: Britannica 'Iron Guard'; Ioanid (2000); 1937 election results.

text: First World War commander, celebrated as the victor of Verdun (1916), who headed the collaborationist Vichy regime from 1940 to 1944. Sentenced to death in 1945, he had the sentence commuted by de Gaulle to life imprisonment because of his age, and died in prison.
method: Balance review: why he was trusted
problem: Verdun explains why many French people trusted him in 1940 (§2).

text: Economist who ruled Portugal as prime minister from 1932 to 1968 and built the authoritarian, Catholic and corporatist Estado Novo. Supporters credit him with stabilizing public finances and keeping Portugal neutral in the Second World War; critics point to the PIDE political police, censorship, the Tarrafal prison camp, poverty and illiteracy, and colonial wars in Africa from 1961. Historians debate whether his regime was fascist; he suppressed Portugal’s own fascist movement in 1934.
method: Balance review: supporters and critics; conf rates the core claim
problem: conf should rate the biographical claim, which is Established; the fascist label is the contested part and is already flagged in the text. Supporters' and critics' cases added. Sources: Britannica 'Salazar'; Costa Pinto; Meneses, Salazar (2009).

text: German-born Jewish girl who hid with her family in Amsterdam from 1942 and kept a diary. The family was arrested in August 1944 after a tip-off whose source is still unknown; she died in the Bergen-Belsen camp in early 1945, and her diary was published in 1947. The people who helped hide the family, including Miep Gies, were later honoured for it.
method: Balance review: uncertainty stated; rescuers named
problem: 'Betrayed' states as known what is still unknown. Adds the helpers (rescuers). Sources: Anne Frank House.

notes: Overall the brief is strong on settled facts (the Holocaust stated plainly; denial confined to a separate page; low estimators like Hata separated from deniers) and on the definitional and Holocaust-history debates. Main balance problems: (1) STRUCTURE PARITY: §1 requires every ideology to show what it promised and the 'gains' as supporters saw them; the brief has no tab for claimed achievements (German unemployment fall, Italian land reclamation and the Lateran Pacts, Franco-era growth, Salazar's finances) tested against evidence (Tooze, Aly, Corner). Without it the dive is not comparable with the Marxism and capitalism dives. (2) ASYMMETRIES inside debates: Goldhagen gets critics but Browning does not; the totalitarianism school gets critics but no 'strength'; the 'right' side of 3B is labelled 'mainstream' and the true/false card gives a verdict; the 'socialist' case omits its best scholars (Zitelmann, Schoenbaum; Italy's IRI). The no-generic-fascism school (Allardyce 1979; Duus and Okimoto on Japan) and Linz's authoritarian/totalitarian distinction are missing. (3) WHY is Germany-centred: no causes for Italy, Spain, Romania, Croatia, Hungary, Japan; missing primary evidence of motives (Abel's 1934 essays, Sopade and SD reports), women (Koonz), churches, Versailles debate (Keynes vs MacMillan/Marks), Fein on why victimization rates differed. Psychology layer must cite replication critiques of Milgram/Zimbardo. (4) MISSING CASES: Slovakia, Bulgaria, Norway/Quisling, Netherlands, Belgium (Rex), Baltic and Ukrainian collaboration (Jedwabne, Arajs Kommando, OUN and Volhynia, each debate shown both ways), Austrofascism, Greece (Metaxas), Brazil's Integralists and Argentina in their own records; Latin America is in the family tree but not in Cases. (5) MISSING VICTIMS: political prisoners (KPD, SPD, unions), forced sterilization (about 400,000), Black Germans and Black French soldiers, Belarus (Khatyn), Warsaw 1944, Leningrad, Greek famine and reprisals, Italian occupation crimes in Yugoslavia (Rab), Italian military internees, Libyan Jews, comfort women (with context on the euphemism), Asian forced labor, Burma railway, Manila, Spanish exiles in Mauthausen, Portugal's colonial wars. (6) OTHER SIDES' VIOLENCE stated factually without equivalence: Chetnik massacres, Bleiburg and the foibe, Italian 1945 reprisals, Katyn, the 1945–50 expulsions of Germans; mostly absent from claim records. (7) LABELS needing context: Il Duce, Führer, Caudillo, Poglavnik, Conducător, Final Solution, 'euthanasia', Kristallnacht, Porajmos (some Roma reject the word), comfort women, Co-Prosperity Sphere, pacification, Valley of the Fallen, 'first victim', 'brava gente', 'Spanish Holocaust' (Preston's title), 'banality of evil'. (8) MODERN PARTIES: AfD, MSI/FdI records now follow the own-statement + critics/authorities template; 3G should add Laruelle (Is Russia Fascist?, 2021) as a 'careful' voice on Russia, the Ukrainian 'ruscism' label alongside Russia's 'denazification', Habermas's 1967 'left fascism', and should apply the template to any named politician (Trump: his and supporters' rejection of the label alongside Paxton and Stanley). (9) MEDIA: Picasso's Guernica is in copyright (link only); set a rule for perpetrator-made photos (Stroop Report, Auschwitz Album) versus forbidden execution images. New facts added in these fixes carry no sources in this file; each 'problem' names what must be sourced before the merge. Two plain fact errors found: Mockler is British, not Italian (Yekatit 12); Bucharest pogrom toll is about 120-125, not 'dozens'. Fact-checker should also check: Unit 731 name date ('from 1936'), and Nuremberg Laws' grandparent definition (supplementary decree of 14 Nov 1935).
